Mastering (5-6 marks): Two well-developed reasons; source of authority named AND developed (e.g. the Pali Canon / Tipitaka; Jataka 075; the Dhammapada on the Eightfold Path); both reasons developed with 'because' or 'this means that'; sub-tradition noted where relevant.

Secure (3-4 marks): Two reasons present, source reference present but partially developed.

Developing (2 marks): One reason developed or two stated without 'because' reasoning; little or no source.

Emerging (1 mark): A basic relevant point with minimal development.

Acceptable reasons:
- The Four Noble Truths provide a practical diagnosis and cure: they identify suffering (dukkha), its cause (tanha rooted in the Three Poisons), its possible cessation (nibbana), and the path to that cessation (the Eightfold Path). The Tipitaka records the Buddha's first teaching at Sarnath as proclaiming these truths, giving them the highest authority.
- The Four Noble Truths are universal in scope: they apply to all human beings regardless of background, because suffering, craving and the possibility of liberation are features of all unenlightened existence. This is why Buddhism is described as open to all — the Dhamma is not restricted to any caste, gender or nationality.

practice_questions.text:
'The life of the Buddha is more important than his teachings.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Buddhist teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Balanced, well-argued response with multiple developed points for and against; Buddhist sources cited on both sides (e.g. Jataka 075 on the Four Sights; the Tipitaka on the Four Noble Truths; the Dhammapada); a JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION stating which side is stronger and why. Accurate SPaG with varied vocabulary.

Secure (7-9 marks): Most points present, source included but not fully developed; conclusion present but weighing incomplete.

Developing (4-6 marks): Largely one-sided; reasoning present but undeveloped; source weak.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points with little development; no conclusion.

Arguments in support:
- The story of the Buddha's life provides a living model: the Four Sights show a human being responding to the reality of suffering, and his Enlightenment demonstrates that liberation is genuinely possible for a human person, not just a divine being. Without this narrative example, the Four Noble Truths might seem abstract.
- Buddhists express devotion to the Buddha as one of the Three Jewels ('I take refuge in the Buddha'), which goes beyond intellectual assent to his teachings. The narrative of the Great Renunciation inspires sacrifice and commitment.
- The story of the Middle Way (between luxury and extreme asceticism) arose from lived experience, not from doctrinal reasoning; this experiential authenticity gives the narrative a practical authority that abstract teachings alone lack.

Arguments against:
- The Buddha himself taught that his life story was not the point: 'Those who see the Dhamma see me; those who see me see the Dhamma.' The teachings (the Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Path) are what bring liberation, not devotion to the teacher's biography.
- The Four Noble Truths have universal application and have guided practitioners across 2,500 years and many cultures where the biographical details of Siddhartha Gautama may vary; the teachings are the transferable element.
- The Pali Canon (Tipitaka) preserves the Dhamma in detail; without these teachings, the story of the Buddha's life would be merely historical rather than spiritually transformative.

Conclusion: a justified conclusion must state which side is stronger and give a reason. Both conclusions are defensible; what matters is that the weighing is explicit and reasoned.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes what Wesak commemorates?
A) The founding of the Sangha at Sarnath
B) The birth, Enlightenment and parinibbana of the Buddha
C) The day the Buddha first taught the Five Precepts
D) The anniversary of the writing of the Tipitaka
practice_questions.marks: B) The birth, Enlightenment and parinibbana of the Buddha [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the date on which Parinirvana Day is observed in most Mahayana Buddhist traditions.
practice_questions.marks: 15 February [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between the way Wesak and Parinirvana Day are observed by Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 2 marks per difference: 1 mark for stating the difference; 2 marks for stating and developing it. Acceptable: Wesak is a joyful celebration including processions, lanterns and offerings; Parinirvana Day is a more reflective occasion focused on meditation on impermanence. Wesak is observed by both Theravada and Mahayana Buddhists; Parinirvana Day is primarily a Mahayana observance. Wesak celebrates all three major life events of the Buddha; Parinirvana Day marks specifically the Buddha's death.

practice_questions.text: Priya's grandmother has recently died. Priya's family are Theravada Buddhists in east London. Explain two things the family might do to mark her death and explain the significance of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. 2 marks per practice: 1 mark for naming the practice; 2 marks for naming it and explaining its significance.

Acceptable answers:
- Inviting monks to chant from the Pali Canon at the home or vihara: the chanting supports the deceased's transition and earns merit for the family who provide hospitality (dana) to the monks. It also embeds the mourning period in the Dhamma, reminding the family of the Buddha's teaching on impermanence.
- Performing meritorious acts in the grandmother's name (giving to the vihara, feeding monks, offering robes): merit is understood to benefit the deceased's next rebirth; this is also an expression of love and ongoing relationship with the deceased.
- Cremation following the tradition of the Buddha's parinibbana: reflects Theravada practice and the teaching of impermanence — the physical body is impermanent and returns to the elements.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why festivals such as Wesak are important for Buddhists in Britain today.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of Buddhist teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two well-developed reasons; source named AND developed (e.g. the Tipitaka on the Buddha's parinibbana; the three events commemorated at Wesak; the Buddha's final teaching on anicca); both reasons developed with 'because' or 'this means that'; reference to Buddhist community in Britain.

Secure (3-4 marks): Two reasons present; source present but not fully developed.

Developing (2 marks): One reason developed, or two stated without development; source absent.

Emerging (1 mark): A basic relevant point.

Acceptable reasons:
- Wesak reinforces core Buddhist beliefs through celebration: because it commemorates the birth, Enlightenment and parinibbana of the Buddha in a single event, it is an annual reminder of the entire arc of the Buddhist path — from a human birth, through the possibility of Enlightenment, to death. The Tipitaka records all three events as central to Buddhist tradition.
- Festivals strengthen Sangha (community): because Wesak gatherings at temples such as Wat Buddhapadipa in London bring together practitioners from Theravada, Mahayana and other traditions, they reinforce the third Jewel — the Sangha — as a source of support and identity for Buddhists living as a minority community in Britain.

practice_questions.text:
'How a Buddhist dies is more important than how they live.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Buddhist teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Balanced response with multiple developed points for and against; Buddhist sources cited on both sides (e.g. Tipitaka on kamma and rebirth; the Bardo Thodol on the dying moment; the Eightfold Path as the guide for how to live); a JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION stating which side is stronger with a reason. Accurate SPaG.

Secure (7-9 marks): Most points present; source included but partially developed; conclusion present.

Developing (4-6 marks): Largely one-sided; some reasoning; source weak.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points; no conclusion.

Arguments in support:
- The dying moment determines the conditions of the next birth: Buddhist teaching holds that the mental state at the moment of death creates the kammic conditions for rebirth. A moment of clarity, compassion or devotion at death can redirect the whole trajectory of future existence. This is why Tibetan Buddhist practice devotes so much attention to the bardo (the state between death and rebirth) and why the Bardo Thodol is read to the dying.
- In Pure Land Buddhism, the sincerity of reciting Amitabha Buddha's name at the moment of death is held to bring rebirth in the Pure Land, regardless of the quality of one's whole life. This places enormous weight on the dying moment.

Arguments against:
- The quality of the dying moment is determined by the quality of the whole life: Buddhist teaching on kamma emphasises that intentional actions throughout a lifetime shape the mental habits and orientations that arise at the moment of death. A person who has cultivated compassion, generosity and mindfulness throughout their life will naturally tend to those qualities at death. The Eightfold Path is a path for living, not just for dying.
- The Five Moral Precepts, the Threefold Way (sila, samadhi, panna) and the cultivation of metta and karuna are guides for daily life, not just for the deathbed. The Buddha's ministry of forty-five years was devoted entirely to teaching how to live.
- Non-Buddhist views might hold that the quality of one's contribution to others throughout a life is what matters morally, not the state of mind at the moment of death.

Conclusion: a justified conclusion must state which side is stronger and give a reason.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes karma in Hindu belief?
A) A fixed destiny decided by God before birth
B) The moral consequences of intentional actions across lifetimes
C) The inner self that passes from body to body at death
D) Liberation from the cycle of birth and death
practice_questions.marks: B) The moral consequences of intentional actions across lifetimes [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: What is the Hindu term for the cycle of birth, death and rebirth?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: samsara.

practice_questions.text: Give two ways in which belief in karma might influence how a Hindu lives.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per way (1 for identification, 1 for development). Acceptable content: a Hindu may practise ahimsa (non-harm) because harming others generates negative karma; a Hindu may perform duties selflessly (karma yoga) because the Bhagavad Gita teaches that action without attachment produces less binding karma; a Hindu may be vegetarian because ahimsa extends to animals; a Hindu may practise regular puja to accumulate good karma and purify past actions.

practice_questions.text:
Rohit is a 17-year-old Vaishnavite Hindu who has just started studying the Bhagavad Gita at his mandir in Leicester. He asks his teacher why the Gita says the atman cannot be destroyed.
Explain two Hindu beliefs about the nature of the atman.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per belief (1 for identification, 1 for development). Acceptable beliefs: the atman is eternal and cannot be destroyed (Bhagavad Gita teaching); the atman is distinct from the body and mind; the atman passes through samsara from body to body; the atman is ultimately related to or identical with Brahman (naming a school such as Advaita earns development credit).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Hindu beliefs about liberation (moksha).
Refer to a sacred writing or another source of Hindu belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed beliefs about moksha with well-integrated source (e.g. Bhagavad Gita on performing duty without attachment as a path to liberation; Upanishadic teaching on atman and Brahman; naming Advaita Vedanta or Vaishnavism to show different understandings of what moksha means). Development uses 'because', 'this means that', 'as a result'. Secure: Two beliefs present, source referenced but partially developed. Developing: Beliefs stated without development; source absent or generic ('Hindu scripture'). Emerging: Basic description of samsara with no source.

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in karma is the most important Hindu belief because it explains all suffering.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Hindu teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Karma provides a coherent explanation for why individuals experience different life circumstances; it offers a framework for understanding suffering as the result of past moral actions rather than random chance. It also motivates ethical behaviour — the knowledge that actions have consequences encourages righteous living. The Bhagavad Gita places karma at the centre of its teaching (karma yoga). Arguments against: Other Hindu beliefs are equally or more central: atman (the eternal self) and moksha (liberation) are the fundamental goals; Brahman as ultimate reality is the basis of all Hindu philosophy. The concept of divine grace (especially in Vaishnavism) suggests that liberation does not depend solely on karma — devotion to God (bhakti) can transcend accumulated karma. Many Hindus would say that ignorance (avidya), not karma itself, is the root cause of suffering. Non-religious view: A humanist might argue that suffering is better explained through natural, social and economic causes than through metaphysical moral causation — and that understanding these causes is more likely to reduce suffering. Justified conclusion: Top-band answers should argue that karma is an important Hindu belief but not the only one; most Hindu traditions would place Brahman, atman and moksha as the foundational framework within which karma operates. The statement is therefore partly true but overstated. Mastering: Full range, sources named, sub-tradition contrast, justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, conclusion. Developing: One-sided. Emerging: Basic description.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following statements best describes the Catholic belief about the Incarnation?
A) Jesus was a great human teacher who was later declared to be God by the Church
B) The eternal Son of God became fully human in Jesus of Nazareth while remaining fully God
C) God briefly appeared as a human but did not genuinely experience human life
D) Jesus was the most perfect human being but was not divine
practice_questions.marks: B) The eternal Son of God became fully human in Jesus of Nazareth while remaining fully God [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the event in which Jesus returned to the Father forty days after the resurrection.
practice_questions.marks: The Ascension [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two contrasting Christian beliefs about how the death of Jesus brings salvation.
For each belief, give a brief development.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per belief (1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point).
Acceptable points include:
- Catholic teaching understands the death of Jesus as an act of atonement — a sacrifice that restores the broken relationship between humanity and God; this sacrifice is made present at every Mass through the Eucharist, which is why the Mass is central to Catholic life.
- Many Protestant traditions emphasise substitutionary atonement — Jesus took the punishment humanity deserved in humanity's place; this means salvation is received through faith in what Christ did, not through sacraments or works.
- Orthodox Christianity sees the cross as the victory of life over death and the beginning of theosis — transformation into the divine life; salvation is a process of becoming more Christlike rather than a legal transaction.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the resurrection of Jesus is important for Catholic Christians.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two fully developed reasons; at least one named source integrated into the argument (e.g. 1 Corinthians 15:17, John 1:14, the Nicene Creed); both reasons clearly connected to significance for Catholic belief or life.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two reasons present, accurate; source present but partially developed.
Developing (2 marks): One reason developed or two briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1 mark): Basic relevant point; no source.

Acceptable points include:
- The resurrection confirms the truth of everything Jesus taught and promised — Paul states 'If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins' (1 Corinthians 15:17); without the resurrection, the Christian hope of salvation would have no foundation.
- The resurrection is the basis of Catholic hope for life after death — because Jesus rose bodily, Catholics believe that they too will share in resurrection; this transforms how Catholics approach death and gives meaning to suffering.
- The resurrection confirms the identity of Jesus as the Son of God and validates his atoning death — the Nicene Creed celebrates that he 'rose again on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures', making the resurrection central to Trinitarian faith.

practice_questions.text:
'The death of Jesus on the cross is more important than his resurrection for Catholic Christians.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Catholic teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Balanced evaluation; accurate Catholic teaching on atonement, resurrection, ascension; named sources (Romans 5:8, 1 Corinthians 15:17, John 1:14, Nicene Creed); sub-tradition contrast (Catholic vs Protestant on atonement models); justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present; source cited; conclusion reached.
Developing (4-6 marks): One-sided or both sides briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points, no sources, no conclusion.

Arguments in support:
- Paul's language in Romans 5:8 focuses on the sacrificial death as the moment of reconciliation: 'Christ died for us.' The Mass re-presents this sacrifice — suggesting the death is the pivotal act.
- Some theological traditions (e.g. substitutionary atonement, prominent in evangelical Protestantism) emphasise that the cross is where sin is dealt with; the resurrection confirms this but does not achieve it.
- Catholic devotional life (the Stations of the Cross, the crucifix in every church) focuses heavily on the passion and death, suggesting the death holds particular weight.

Arguments against:
- Paul also insists: 'If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile' (1 Corinthians 15:17) — without the resurrection, the death has no ultimate power.
- The resurrection is the basis of hope for believers — it shows that death is not the end and that Jesus's redemptive work is complete and victorious.
- Catholic teaching on grace and salvation is grounded in the risen Christ sending the Spirit; without the resurrection and ascension, there would be no Church, no sacraments, and no ongoing communication of grace.

Conclusion: Candidates may argue either side. A strong conclusion will acknowledge that Catholics themselves hold both together: 'We proclaim your death, O Lord, and profess your resurrection' (the Memorial Acclamation at Mass), suggesting neither alone is sufficient.

practice_questions.text:
Caitlin is a Catholic teenager attending Mass with her family at a parish in Liverpool. She notices the large crucifix at the front of the church. Give two reasons why the crucifix is an important symbol in a Catholic church.
For each reason, give a brief development.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point).
Acceptable points include:
- It represents the atoning death of Jesus — the sacrifice that reconciles humanity to God.
- It is a reminder of God's love for humanity — 'while we were still sinners, Christ died for us' (Romans 5:8).
- It keeps the passion of Jesus at the centre of Catholic worship and devotion.
- It reminds Catholics that the Mass re-presents the sacrifice of the cross.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct reference for the Ten Commandments in the Torah?
A) Genesis 12:1-3
B) Deuteronomy 6:4
C) Exodus 20:1-17
D) Leviticus 19:18
practice_questions.marks: C) Exodus 20:1-17 [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the prophet who received the Torah from God at Sinai.
practice_questions.marks: Moses [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give one promise God made to Abraham in Genesis 12:1-3.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for one correct promise. Acceptable answers: a land (Canaan, the promised land); many descendants (a great nation); blessing for all the families of the earth.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the Covenant at Sinai is important in Jewish belief and practice.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed reasons, each with explanation and development. At least one named source cited (Exodus 20:1-17; the Torah; the Ten Commandments). Sub-tradition contrast or application to daily life strengthens the answer. Example: 'The Covenant at Sinai is important because it gave the entire Jewish people a framework for living — the 613 mitzvot, including the Ten Commandments in Exodus 20:1-17, which means that every aspect of daily life becomes an act of obedience to God and a fulfilment of the covenant.' Secure: Both reasons present, source cited. Developing: One reason developed. Emerging: Basic points only.

practice_questions.text:
'The Covenant with Abraham is more important to Jewish belief than the Covenant at Sinai.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Jewish teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The Abraham Covenant is the oldest and most foundational — it establishes the identity of the Jewish people as God's chosen people and promises them a land and a future (Genesis 12:1-3). Without Abraham there is no Sinai — the covenant with Abraham creates the people who will later receive the Torah. The physical sign of Brit Milah (circumcision) makes it an embodied, lifelong commitment. Arguments against: The Sinai covenant encompasses the whole people, not just one individual and his family; it gives the Jewish people their entire way of life through the Torah and the 613 mitzvot, including the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:1-17). Jewish daily life is structured around the Sinai covenant — prayer, Shabbat, festivals, dietary laws all flow from it. Moses — the mediator of the Sinai covenant — is the greatest of all Jewish prophets. Non-religious view: A humanist might argue that neither covenant is literally true but that the ethical teachings they generated (justice, care for the poor, respect for life) are what matter. Justified conclusion required. Mastering: Balanced, developed arguments; sources on both sides; justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, source present, conclusion present but not fully reasoned. Developing: One side developed; weak conclusion. Emerging: Basic, listing, no conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Levi is a 14-year-old at a Jewish school in north London. His teacher explains that the Ten Commandments are divided into two types. Explain two differences between the two types of commandment.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark per difference identified, 1 mark for each developed. Mitzvot between man and God (bein adam l'Makom) govern the individual's relationship with God — e.g. Shabbat, prayer, dietary laws — sanctifying the divine relationship (2 marks). Mitzvot between man and man (bein adam l'chavero) govern relationships with other people — e.g. not stealing, caring for the poor, honesty — sanctifying communal life (2 marks).

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the chuppah at a Jewish wedding?
A) The marriage contract setting out the groom's obligations
B) The wedding canopy symbolising the new home the couple is creating
C) The seven blessings recited over wine during the ceremony
D) The prayer of praise recited by mourners at synagogue
practice_questions.marks: B) The wedding canopy symbolising the new home the couple is creating [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the seven-day mourning period in Judaism following a burial.
practice_questions.marks: Shiva [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two contrasting ways in which Bat Mitzvah is celebrated in Orthodox and Reform Jewish communities.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark per practice identified, 1 mark per development. In Orthodox communities, girls do not read from the Torah in the main synagogue service; they may mark the occasion through a ceremony or a talk, because traditional Orthodox practice restricts Torah leadership to men (2 marks). In Reform and Liberal communities, girls read from the Torah on equal terms with boys, reflecting the belief that women have the same religious status and responsibilities as men (2 marks).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the Bar and Bat Mitzvah ceremony is important in Jewish life.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed reasons with named sources. Sources: Genesis 17 (covenant with Abraham, into which the child enters at birth through Brit Milah; Bar/Bat Mitzvah extends this to personal responsibility for the mitzvot); Exodus 20 (the Ten Commandments, for which the Bar/Bat Mitzvah child now takes personal responsibility); the principle that the mitzvot are the Jewish way of life from which no adult is exempt. Sub-tradition contrast on Bat Mitzvah practice adds depth. Secure: Two reasons, source cited. Developing: One reason developed. Emerging: Basic points.

practice_questions.text:
'The most important Jewish life-cycle ceremony is the Bar or Bat Mitzvah.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Jewish teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Bar/Bat Mitzvah marks the moment of full religious adulthood — from this point the individual is personally responsible for all 613 mitzvot, making it the defining transition in Jewish religious life. It is the first major ceremony the individual themselves participates in fully (not just being done to them, as in Brit Milah). Torah reading in public for the first time is a profound expression of belonging to the Jewish covenant community. Arguments against: Brit Milah could be considered more foundational because it is rooted in the oldest covenant (Genesis 17) and marks entry into the Jewish people at birth — without it, the Bar Mitzvah has no covenant context. Marriage creates the Jewish home, which is the mikdash me'at (little sanctuary) at the heart of Jewish life; death and mourning rituals (shiva, kaddish) give Judaism its most profound expression of faith under pressure. Non-religious view: A humanist might value all these ceremonies for their social function (community cohesion, marking transition) rather than their religious content, and might consider coming-of-age rituals universally important regardless of religion. Justified conclusion required. Mastering: Balanced, developed; sources on both sides; justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, source, conclusion. Developing: One side. Emerging: Listing, no conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Isaac is preparing for his Bar Mitzvah at an Orthodox synagogue in north London. Give one thing Isaac will need to do to be ready for his Bar Mitzvah service.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for one correct preparation. Acceptable answers: learn to read a portion of the Torah in Hebrew (the parashah); learn the Haftarah, the related passage from the Prophets; learn the blessings said before and after the Torah reading.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the meaning of the Holika Dahan bonfire at Holi?
A) It represents the burning of old clothes to welcome spring
B) It symbolises the destruction of the demoness Holika and the triumph of devotion over evil
C) It is a secular celebration of the end of winter
D) It represents Rama's victory over the demon Ravana
practice_questions.marks: B) It symbolises the destruction of the demoness Holika and the triumph of devotion over evil [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the goddess whose worship is central to the main night of Diwali.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Lakshmi.

practice_questions.text: Give two ways in which Diwali is celebrated by Hindus in Britain today.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per way (1 for identification, 1 for development). Acceptable answers: lighting of diyas and candles in the home to welcome Lakshmi; performance of Lakshmi puja on the main night; decoration of homes with rangoli; exchange of gifts and sweets; community gatherings and processions (e.g. Leicester's Belgrave Road celebrations); fireworks; visiting the mandir for special puja services.

practice_questions.text:
Parveen is a 15-year-old Hindu girl preparing for Holi with her family in Birmingham. She asks her grandmother why the festival involves throwing coloured powder.
Explain two reasons why the throwing of colours at Holi is meaningful for Hindus.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for identification, 1 for development). Acceptable reasons: the colours recall the playful story of Krishna and Radha at Vrindavan — the joyful expression of bhakti love; the throwing of colours on all people equally symbolises that before God all are equal — social distinctions are dissolved during Holi; the festival celebrates the arrival of spring and the renewal of the natural world, which Hindus understand as God's creation; the colour represents the exuberance and joy of devotion.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why Diwali is an important festival for Hindus.
Refer to a sacred writing or another source of Hindu belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed reasons with a named source integrated. Primary source: the Ramayana (Rama's return to Ayodhya after defeating Ravana — the lighting of lamps celebrated his return and the triumph of righteousness). Reason 1: Diwali reaffirms core Hindu beliefs about dharma — Rama's story teaches that truth and righteousness will ultimately triumph over evil, giving worshippers confidence in the cosmic moral order. Reason 2: Lakshmi puja connects the festival to daily Hindu life — the prayers for prosperity and wellbeing at Diwali reflect the purushartha of artha (material wellbeing as a legitimate aim of life), and the lighting of the home symbolises inviting divine grace into everyday existence. Sub-tradition contrast (different Diwali stories in Vaishnavite/South Indian traditions) earns further credit. Secure: Two reasons, source referenced. Developing: One reason without development. Emerging: Basic description of practices.

practice_questions.text:
'Holi is a more important festival than Diwali for Hindus in Britain today.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Hindu teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Holi's themes of equality, joy and the renewal of community may be especially resonant for British Hindus living in a multicultural society where social divisions are a daily reality. Holi has grown significantly in public visibility in Britain — university events, Bhaktivedanta Manor's Holi celebration. Holi's joyful, accessible character may appeal to younger generations and bridge Hindu and non-Hindu communities in a way that Diwali's domestic puja does not. Arguments against: Diwali is far more widely recognised as a Hindu festival in British public life and has greater public impact (Leicester's celebrations, public lighting events, Diwali cards). The religious depth of Diwali — Lakshmi puja, the return of Rama — gives it a more explicitly devotional character. For most Hindu families in Britain, Diwali is the festival at which the whole family gathers and which most directly expresses devotion to God through puja. The Ramayana's story of Rama's return is one of the most beloved narratives in the Hindu tradition and gives Diwali deep theological grounding. Non-religious view: A humanist might value both festivals for their community-building functions and the joy they bring, without accepting their theological claims. Justified conclusion: Top-band answers should argue that both festivals serve important but different functions — Diwali is more central to formal devotional practice and cultural identity in Britain, while Holi is increasingly important for community integration and for younger Hindus. The statement is therefore an overstatement — both are important, serving different needs. Mastering: Full range, named sources, sub-tradition contrast, justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, conclusion. Developing: One-sided. Emerging: Description only.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes sanatana dharma?
A) The duty appropriate to one's caste and life stage
B) The eternal way or eternal religion — the universal principles of Hindu teaching
C) The cycle of birth, death and rebirth
D) Liberation from the cycle of samsara
practice_questions.marks: B) The eternal way or eternal religion — the universal principles of Hindu teaching [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name one of the four aims of human life (purusharthas) in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: dharma, artha, kama, moksha.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the concept of dharma influences how Hindus live.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per way (1 for identification, 1 for development). Acceptable content: dharma as the ethical framework for pursuing artha and kama — a Hindu will not pursue wealth through deception because this transgresses dharma; dharma as role-specific duty — a Hindu parent has the dharma of raising children well; dharma as the framework for the four stages of life (student, householder, retirement, renunciation); dharma shaping daily conduct through practices like ahimsa.

practice_questions.text:
Sanjay is a 40-year-old Hindu businessman in Leeds. He is deciding whether to accept a contract that would earn him significant money but would involve deceiving a customer.
Explain how the concept of dharma might guide Sanjay's decision.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 for identifying dharma as ethical duty; 1 for explaining that artha (wealth) must be pursued within the bounds of dharma; 1 for development (e.g. the Bhagavad Gita's teaching on righteous action; or that deception generates negative karma); 1 for a conclusion about Sanjay's decision. Credit for: naming the Bhagavad Gita; naming the purushartha framework; linking karma to the decision.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why dharma is important in Hindu belief.
Refer to a sacred writing or another source of Hindu belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two developed reasons (e.g. dharma as the cosmic and moral order that holds the universe together — when Vishnu restores dharma through avatars, the Bhagavad Gita exemplifies this; dharma as individual duty — the Bhagavad Gita teaches that performing one's duty without attachment is the highest form of righteous action and the path to liberation). Source well-integrated. Sub-tradition contrast (varnashrama dharma varying by context; bhakti vs karma yoga approaches to dharma) earns further credit. Secure: Two reasons, source referenced. Developing: Reasons stated without development. Emerging: Basic description of duty.

practice_questions.text:
'Moksha is the most important of the four aims of human life for Hindus.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Hindu teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Moksha is the ultimate goal of the soul's journey through samsara — the Bhagavad Gita and the Upanishads both identify liberation as the highest human aspiration. The four life stages (ashramas) culminate in sannyasa (renunciation), where moksha is the exclusive focus. Moksha is the only aim that is truly permanent — artha and kama are temporary satisfactions. Arguments against: Dharma is the framework for all four aims — without it, artha and kama become harmful. For most Hindus in the householder stage of life, dharma (fulfilling one's duties to family, community and cosmos) and artha (supporting one's family) are the practically central aims. The tradition affirms that artha and kama are legitimate and important; to neglect them would be to deny the value of ordinary human life. Many Hindus would say that living virtuously (dharma) is itself the most important daily expression of their faith. Non-religious view: A humanist might argue that the idea of liberation from a cycle of rebirth is metaphysical and unverifiable; from a humanist perspective, well-being and flourishing in this life are the primary goals — closer to artha and kama than to moksha. Justified conclusion: A top-band answer will argue that while moksha is the ultimate spiritual goal, it does not override the practical centrality of dharma for most Hindus in daily life; the four aims work together, with dharma as the ethical framework and moksha as the final destination. The statement is partly true but does not capture the balance the tradition teaches. Mastering: Full range, sources named, sub-tradition contrasts, justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, source, conclusion. Developing: One-sided. Emerging: Lists rather than evaluates.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes bhakti yoga?
A) The path of meditation through the eight-limbed practice of Patanjali
B) The path of selfless action performed without attachment to results
C) The path of loving devotion to a personal God, expressed through prayer and worship
D) The path of philosophical inquiry into the nature of atman and Brahman
practice_questions.marks: C) The path of loving devotion to a personal God, expressed through prayer and worship [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the sacred city on the banks of the Ganges that is considered the holiest place in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Varanasi (accept: Kashi, Benares).

practice_questions.text: Give two differences between karma yoga and bhakti yoga.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per difference (1 for identification, 1 for development). Acceptable answers: karma yoga focuses on selfless action/service as the path to God; bhakti yoga focuses on loving devotion through prayer, puja and worship — (1). Karma yoga is suited to active, engaged personalities; bhakti yoga is suited to those drawn to personal relationship with God — (2). Karma yoga sees work as an offering to God; bhakti yoga sees love and devotion as the direct path — (3). Advaita teachers may favour jnana yoga; Vaishnavite traditions favour bhakti yoga — showing sub-tradition differences — (3 or 4).

practice_questions.text:
Vikram is a 35-year-old Hindu software engineer in Manchester. He volunteers every weekend at a Hindu food bank, serving food to homeless people. He describes this as 'my yoga'.
Explain how Vikram's volunteering can be understood as a Hindu spiritual practice.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 for identifying karma yoga; 1 for explaining the principle (selfless action without attachment to reward is an offering to God); 1 for the Bhagavad Gita's teaching (perform duty without attachment to fruit); 1 for development (service to others is service to God because the divine is present in all beings; Vikram's action generates positive karma while purifying his ego).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why pilgrimage is important for Hindus.
Refer to a sacred writing or another source of Hindu belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed reasons with a named source. Reason 1: pilgrimage to Varanasi offers the possibility of moksha — the sacred city is where the divine is especially present; Shiva is said to whisper the liberation mantra to the dying. Source: the Hindu tradition teaches that Varanasi is the abode of Shiva; the Ganges (associated with Vishnu's feet in some traditions) is believed to wash away all karma. Reason 2: Kumbh Mela demonstrates the universality and communal power of Hindu faith — tens of millions gather, crossing caste, region and sub-tradition, united in the act of pilgrimage and sacred bathing. Source: the Bhagavad Gita's teaching that God accepts sincere devotion from all paths — the act of pilgrimage is an act of devotion (bhakti) accessible to all. Secure: Two reasons, source referenced. Developing: Reasons stated without development. Emerging: Basic factual description.

practice_questions.text:
'Bhakti yoga is the most important of the four yogas for Hindus today.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Hindu teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The Bhagavad Gita (chapter 12) explicitly states that those who fix their minds on God with constant devotion are the best yogis, suggesting bhakti is the highest path. Bhakti yoga is by far the most widely practised path among Hindus today — in Vaishnavite and Shaivite traditions, devotion through puja, bhajan and pilgrimage is the primary form of practice. Bhakti yoga is accessible to all regardless of education or physical ability; it requires only sincere love for God. ISKCON at Bhaktivedanta Manor represents the global reach of bhakti yoga practice. Arguments against: The Bhagavad Gita also states that all four paths are valid and that God accepts sincere devotion through any path. Jnana yoga, as the path of knowledge, is held by Advaita Vedanta teachers (such as Shankara and, later, Ramana Maharshi) to be the most direct route to liberation. Karma yoga is arguably the most practically relevant path for modern Hindus in working and family life — social action, ethical business and community service are all expressions of karma yoga. Astanga yoga (through practices like daily meditation) has gained millions of practitioners globally, including among British Hindus. Non-religious view: A humanist might value the ethical and social dimensions of karma yoga (selfless service) while remaining sceptical of the metaphysical claims of any of the paths. Justified conclusion: Top-band answers should argue that for the majority of practising Hindus today, especially in bhakti-centred Vaishnavite and Shaivite communities, bhakti yoga is indeed the most central practice; but the tradition itself is explicit that all four paths are valid. The statement is partly true but overstates a single path in a tradition that celebrates diversity of approach. Mastering: Full range, named sources, sub-tradition contrasts, justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, conclusion. Developing: One-sided. Emerging: Description only.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct Pali term for the Buddhist quality of loving kindness?
A) Karuna
B) Metta
C) Sila
D) Panna
practice_questions.marks: B) Metta [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the first of the Five Moral Precepts observed by lay Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks: Do not take life [1 mark]. Accept: not to take life; refrain from taking life.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which a lay Buddhist might express the quality of karuna (compassion) in their daily life.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 2 marks per way: 1 mark for naming the way; 2 marks for naming it and explaining it. Acceptable: volunteering at a food bank or hospice; prison chaplaincy; adopting a plant-based diet to avoid harming animals; practising metta bhavana (loving kindness meditation) to cultivate goodwill toward those who are difficult; supporting Buddhist charitable organisations.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two contrasting Buddhist beliefs about the importance of ethical action in daily life.
In your answer refer to Theravada and Mahayana Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. 2 marks per belief: 1 mark for a relevant point; 2 marks for a developed point.

Acceptable points:
- Theravada Buddhism emphasises the Five Moral Precepts as the ethical foundation: lay practitioners commit to five restraints from harm. These are grounded in the law of kamma — breaking the Precepts plants harmful seeds in the mind, while observing them cultivates the conditions for liberation. [1-2 marks]
- Mahayana Buddhism develops the Six Perfections: ethics is the second Perfection (morality), but it is embedded alongside generosity, patience, energy, meditation and wisdom. The Bodhisattva practises ethics not only for personal liberation but for the benefit of all sentient beings, driven by karuna and the Bodhisattva vow. [1-2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the Five Moral Precepts are important to Buddhists in Britain today.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of Buddhist teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two well-developed reasons; source named AND developed (e.g. Dhammapada 190-191 on the Noble Eightfold Path as the way to the end of suffering; the Tipitaka on the Five Precepts and kamma); sub-tradition noted where relevant; both reasons developed with 'because' or 'this means that'.

Secure (3-4 marks): Two reasons present; source present but partially developed.

Developing (2 marks): One reason developed, or two stated without development; source absent.

Emerging (1 mark): A basic relevant point.

Acceptable reasons:
- The Precepts are the sila dimension of the Threefold Way: the Dhammapada 190-191 names the Noble Eightfold Path as the way that leads to the end of suffering, and that path works as sila (ethics), samadhi (meditation) and panna (wisdom). Without sila, meditation cannot deepen and wisdom cannot arise. In daily life this means the Precepts are not optional extras but the ethical foundation that makes the whole path possible.
- The Precepts embody karuna (compassion) in concrete form: because all beings experience suffering (dukkha), observing the first Precept (not taking life) and the fifth (not taking intoxicants, which cloud the mind and can lead to harmful behaviour) expresses a commitment to reducing harm for all. This is why Buddhist communities in Britain describe keeping the Precepts as a form of social responsibility, not just individual spiritual practice.

practice_questions.text:
'For Buddhists, the Six Perfections are more important than the Five Moral Precepts in daily life.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Buddhist teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Balanced, well-argued response with multiple developed points for and against; Buddhist sources cited (e.g. Dhammapada 190-191 on the Noble Eightfold Path; Mahayana sutras on the Six Perfections and the Bodhisattva vow); a JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION stating which is more important in daily life with a reason. Accurate SPaG.

Secure (7-9 marks): Most points present; source included but partially developed; conclusion present.

Developing (4-6 marks): Largely one-sided; some reasoning; source weak.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points; no conclusion.

Arguments in support:
- The Six Perfections are more comprehensive: they include morality (which contains the Precepts) plus generosity, patience, energy, meditation and wisdom. A Bodhisattva practising all six is doing more than someone observing only the Precepts. Mahayana tradition holds that the Bodhisattva path is the highest form of Buddhist practice.
- The Six Perfections explicitly aim at the benefit of all beings, not just oneself. Because dependent arising (paticcasamupada) teaches the interconnection of all things, an ethic aimed at universal liberation is more consistent with the Dhamma than one focused on individual restraint.
- The first Perfection (generosity/dana) is not one of the Five Precepts at all; without including generosity in one's ethical life, one is practising an incomplete version of Buddhist ethics.

Arguments against:
- The Five Moral Precepts are the universal ethical foundation for all lay Buddhists, regardless of tradition. The Precepts appear in both Theravada and Mahayana teaching, making them more fundamental to daily life than the Six Perfections, which are a specifically Mahayana teaching.
- For most lay Buddhists, consistently observing the Five Precepts is itself challenging: not lying, not taking intoxicants, not misusing the senses require constant attention. The Precepts are practical and applicable in every situation, whereas the Six Perfections describe a more advanced path.
- The Dhammapada 190-191 names the Noble Eightfold Path as the way to the end of suffering, and that path is grouped as the Threefold Way (sila, samadhi, panna), placing sila — the ethical foundation including the Precepts — as the first and necessary dimension.

Conclusion: a justified conclusion must state which is more important in daily life and give a reason. Both positions are defensible; what matters is the quality of the weighing.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the Khalsa?
A) The eternal scripture of Sikhism
B) The five items worn by all Sikhs
C) The community of initiated Sikhs, founded by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699
D) The free communal meal served at every gurdwara
practice_questions.marks: C) The community of initiated Sikhs, founded by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699 [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the Sikh initiation ceremony in which a person is admitted into the Khalsa.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Amrit Sanskar (accept 'taking amrit').

practice_questions.text: Name one of the five Ks worn by amritdhari Sikhs, using its Punjabi name.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: Kesh (uncut hair); Kangha (wooden comb); Kara (steel bracelet); Kachera (cotton undergarment); Kirpan (ceremonial sword).

practice_questions.text: Explain two contrasting perspectives of amritdhari and sahajdhari Sikhs on the five Ks.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. Students may include:
- Amritdhari Sikhs are initiated into the Khalsa through Amrit Sanskar and are obligated to observe all five Ks as a visible commitment to their faith and community — this means the five Ks are a daily reminder of their covenant with the Guru (1 + 1 marks).
- Sahajdhari Sikhs follow Sikh teaching without formal initiation and are not required to wear the five Ks — this means they may practise sewa, attend the gurdwara and pray without the visible markers of Khalsa membership, although some choose to wear the kara voluntarily (1 + 1 marks).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the Amrit Sanskar ceremony is important to Sikhs.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two developed reasons with reference to the Guru Granth Sahib or Guru Gobind Singh's founding action. Possible points: (1) Amrit Sanskar connects the initiate directly to Guru Gobind Singh's original Panj Pyare — the amrit is prepared while reciting hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib, meaning the ceremony places the initiate under the living Guru's guidance and makes them part of an unbroken community going back to 1699. (2) Amrit Sanskar expresses the Sikh belief in equality — the ceremony is open to any Sikh regardless of caste or background, enacting the Khalsa's founding principle that all are equal before God; this means initiation is both a personal spiritual commitment and a public statement of equality.
Secure (3-4 marks): Reasons present, mostly accurate; source named but underdeveloped.
Developing (1-2 marks): One reason, limited development, source absent.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

practice_questions.text:
'The five Ks are the most important part of being a Sikh.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
- refer to Sikh teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- The five Ks make Sikh identity visible in daily life — wearing Kesh, Kara and Kirpan signals to the world that a person is committed to the Khalsa and its values of equality, service and justice.
- The five Ks connect amritdhari Sikhs to the founding Panj Pyare and to Guru Gobind Singh's vision — they are a living embodiment of Sikh history and tradition.
- Each K carries specific spiritual significance: Kesh (accepting God's creation), Kangha (spiritual discipline), Kara (unity of God), Kachera (self-control), Kirpan (defending the weak) — together they form a comprehensive code of Sikh living.
- For an amritdhari Sikh, the five Ks are a covenant with the Guru Granth Sahib and the Khalsa community — neglecting them would be a breach of their initiation vows.

Arguments against:
- The five Ks are obligations for amritdhari Sikhs only — sahajdhari Sikhs are recognised as sincere Sikhs without the five Ks; this suggests the inner commitment is more important than outward marks.
- Guru Nanak's three pillars (nam japna, kirat karni, vand chakna) pre-date the Khalsa and apply to all Sikhs, suggesting that devotion, honest work and sharing are more fundamental than the five Ks.
- The Guru Granth Sahib (not the five Ks) is the eternal living Guru — sincere relationship with the scripture is arguably more central to Sikh identity.
- Many Sikhs worldwide are sahajdhari yet deeply committed to Sikh values of equality and sewa without the five Ks.

Mastering (10-12 marks): Both sides argued with Sikh sources; amritdhari/sahajdhari distinction used; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present, mostly accurate, some sources, conclusion.
Developing (4-6 marks): Mostly one-sided, limited sources.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points, no sources, no conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the Pali term for the ethical dimension of the Threefold Way?
A) Samadhi
B) Panna
C) Sila
D) Karuna
practice_questions.marks: C) Sila [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the Buddhist text that says that of all paths the Eightfold Path is the best.
practice_questions.marks: The Dhammapada [1 mark]. Accept: Dhammapada 273; the Pali Canon (Tipitaka).

practice_questions.text: Give one of the Five Moral Precepts observed by lay Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for one correctly stated Precept. Any one of: do not take life; do not take what is not given; do not misuse the senses; do not speak falsehoods; do not take intoxicants that cloud the mind.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two different Buddhist beliefs about ethical living.
In your answer refer to Theravada and Mahayana Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. 2 marks per belief: 1 mark for a relevant point; 2 marks for a developed point.

Acceptable points:
- Theravada Buddhism emphasises the Five Moral Precepts and the sila dimension of the Eightfold Path as restraint from harm: not taking life, not stealing, not speaking falsehood. This is framed as the ethical foundation without which meditation and wisdom cannot develop. [1-2 marks]
- Mahayana Buddhism extends this through the Six Perfections: not just restraint from harm but the active cultivation of generosity, patience and wisdom. The Bodhisattva practises ethics as part of the universal mission to liberate all sentient beings, driven by karuna (compassion) and metta (loving kindness). [1-2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why karuna (compassion) is important in Buddhist ethical teaching.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of Buddhist teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two well-developed reasons; source named AND its relevance developed (e.g. Dhammapada 190-191 on the Eightfold Path; the Tipitaka on metta bhavana; Mahayana sutras on the Bodhisattva vow); both reasons use 'because' or 'this means that'; sub-tradition named where relevant.

Secure (3-4 marks): Two reasons present, source present but not fully developed.

Developing (2 marks): One reason developed, or two stated without development; source weak or absent.

Emerging (1 mark): A basic relevant point.

Acceptable reasons:
- Karuna motivates ethical action toward all living beings: because all beings experience suffering (dukkha), compassion means recognising their suffering as equal to one's own and acting to relieve it. This is why the first Precept (not to take life) applies not just to humans but to animals. The Tipitaka records the Buddha teaching karuna as one of the four Brahmaviharas (divine abodes).
- In Mahayana Buddhism, karuna is the foundation of the Bodhisattva vow: the Bodhisattva delays their own liberation because compassion makes it impossible to remain indifferent to the suffering of all sentient beings. Developing karuna through meditation (metta bhavana) and practice transforms the practitioner from a focus on personal liberation to universal service.

practice_questions.text:
'Following the Eightfold Path is the most important thing a Buddhist can do.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Buddhist teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Balanced, well-argued response with multiple developed points for and against; Buddhist sources cited on both sides (e.g. Dhammapada 190-191; the Tipitaka; Mahayana sutras on the Six Perfections); a JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION stating which side is stronger and why. Accurate SPaG.

Secure (7-9 marks): Most points present, source included but partially developed; conclusion present but weighing incomplete.

Developing (4-6 marks): Largely one-sided; reasoning present but undeveloped; source weak.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points with little development; no conclusion.

Arguments in support:
- The Eightfold Path is the Fourth Noble Truth: the practical solution the Buddha identified at his Enlightenment. Without following the path, knowledge of the first three truths (suffering exists, it has a cause, it can cease) remains theoretical. Dhammapada 190-191 names the Noble Eightfold Path as the truth that leads to the cessation of suffering.
- Following the path is not one activity among others but a comprehensive transformation of speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration and wisdom: it covers the whole of life.
- The Five Moral Precepts are the practical expression of the Eightfold Path's ethical dimension (sila) for lay Buddhists; without observing them, the conditions for meditation and wisdom cannot arise.

Arguments against:
- In Mahayana Buddhism, the Bodhisattva path with its Six Perfections might be considered more important: it extends the Eightfold Path from individual liberation to universal liberation, aligning with the teaching of karuna and the interconnectedness of all beings.
- Some Buddhist traditions (Pure Land) hold that devotion to Amitabha Buddha and recitation of his name is more important for lay practitioners than formal Eightfold Path practice, given the difficulties of sustaining rigorous practice in everyday life.
- Other Buddhist practices such as meditation on Buddha-nature (Zen), tantric visualisation (Tibetan Buddhism) or chanting (many Mahayana traditions) are held by their practitioners to be equally if not more central than the formal Eightfold Path structure.

Conclusion: a justified conclusion must weigh these arguments and state which is stronger, giving a reason.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes 'tan sewa' in Sikhism?
A) Donating money to support others
B) Teaching and offering guidance to others
C) Physical service such as cleaning the gurdwara
D) Meditating on the name of God
practice_questions.marks: C) Physical service such as cleaning the gurdwara [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the Sikh term for the religious community or congregation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: sangat.

practice_questions.text: Name one type of sewa in Sikh teaching.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: tan (physical sewa); man (mental sewa); dhan (material sewa).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why sewa is important in Sikhism.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. Students may include:
- Sewa is a form of worship: serving another person is serving the divine light (jot) within them — this means sewa is not merely volunteering but an act of devotion to God (1 + 1 marks).
- Sewa fights haumai (ego): performing humble service without expectation of recognition dismantles self-centredness — this means sewa is also a spiritual discipline that moves the soul towards mukti (1 + 1 marks).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the sangat is important to Sikhs.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two developed reasons with reference to the Guru Granth Sahib or Sikh teaching. Possible points: (1) The sangat is spiritually transforming — the Guru Granth Sahib teaches that being in the company of sincere, God-centred believers strengthens one's own faith; this means the sangat actively supports each member's spiritual journey towards mukti. (2) The sangat is where sewa is practised collectively — through langar, mutual support in times of hardship, and shared worship, the community enacts the Sikh belief in the equality of all people and the importance of service.
Secure (3-4 marks): Reasons present, mostly accurate; source named but underdeveloped.
Developing (1-2 marks): One reason, limited development, source absent.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

practice_questions.text:
'Sewa (service) is more important than prayer for a Sikh.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
- refer to Sikh teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- Sewa is described in the Guru Granth Sahib as a form of worship — not separate from devotion to God but an expression of it; serving another is serving God.
- The three forms of sewa (tan, man, dhan) encompass the whole person — body, mind and resources — making it a comprehensive way of living the faith.
- Langar, the communal meal at every gurdwara, is a visible, public expression of sewa that reaches thousands daily at gurdwaras like the Golden Temple in Amritsar; prayer is private and less immediately transformative for society.
- Sewa directly fights haumai (ego), which is the primary barrier to mukti; prayer, without a change in attitude and action, may not produce the same transformation.

Arguments against:
- Nam japna (meditating on the name of God) is described in the Guru Granth Sahib as the highest spiritual practice — without devotion to God, sewa becomes mere social work rather than worship.
- Nitnem (daily prayers, including the Mool Mantra and Japji Sahib) is a core obligation for amritdhari Sikhs; prayer is the foundation of the spiritual life on which sewa rests.
- Guru Nanak's own life emphasised devotional music (kirtan) and nam simran as central — not sewa alone.
- A person may perform sewa for reputation or social approval rather than for God; the motivation behind sewa (God-centred, not ego-driven) is inseparable from prayer.

Mastering (10-12 marks): Both sides argued with Sikh sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present, mostly accurate, some sources, conclusion.
Developing (4-6 marks): Mostly one-sided, limited sources.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points, no sources, no conclusion.

before.exam_tip_html:
On any question about sewa, make sure you distinguish the three types using their Punjabi terms: tan (physical), man (mental) and dhan (material). Answers that describe sewa only as “helping others” or “volunteering” miss the theological depth — sewa is understood as worship of God, not simply philanthropy. The mark scheme rewards the explanation that serving another person is serving God’s divine light within them.

For the 6-mark Explain question, name the Guru Granth Sahib as your source of authority. You can reference the GGS teaching that serving humanity and serving God are not separate acts, or its teaching that the company of God-centred people strengthens a person’s faith. That counts as a named source. To reach the top band you still need two reasons, each developed.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the term 'trefah' in Jewish dietary law?
A) Food that is permitted according to kashrut
B) The blessing recited before eating a meal
C) Food that is forbidden according to kashrut
D) The separation of milk and meat dishes
practice_questions.marks: C) Food that is forbidden according to kashrut [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the Jewish festival that commemorates the Exodus from Egypt.
practice_questions.marks: Pesach (Passover) [1 mark — accept either name]

practice_questions.text: Give two contrasting Jewish views about the importance of keeping dietary laws (kashrut).
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark per view, 1 mark per development. Orthodox Jews observe kashrut strictly because it is a binding mitzvah from the Torah (Leviticus 11; Exodus 23:19); every meal becomes a religious act that reinforces Jewish identity and the covenant (2 marks). Reform and Liberal Jews approach kashrut with greater personal autonomy; many value the laws' connection to Jewish identity and discipline, but believe individuals should decide how much to observe based on personal conviction rather than strict legal obligation (2 marks).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why Yom Kippur is the most important day in the Jewish calendar.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed reasons with named sources. Sources: Leviticus 23:27-28 (the Torah's command to fast and afflict the soul on Yom Kippur); the Talmud on the nature of teshuvah (repentance); the principle that Yom Kippur atones for sins between humans and God. Development examples: Yom Kippur is the one day in the year when the gates of repentance are considered fully open — missing it means missing the annual opportunity for atonement; the 25-hour fast demonstrates complete submission to God; collective confession (Vidui) unites the Jewish community in shared accountability. Secure: Two reasons, source cited. Developing: One reason developed. Emerging: Basic points.

practice_questions.text:
'Observing kashrut is the most important way for Jews to express their Jewish identity.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Jewish teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Kashrut affects every meal, making it the most frequent and pervasive expression of Jewish identity — three times daily, every day of the year. It is rooted directly in the Torah (Leviticus 11; Exodus 23:19), making it a covenant obligation. It distinguishes Jews in the public sphere (avoiding non-kosher restaurants and food) and creates a distinctive Jewish way of life. Arguments against: Shabbat observance, Torah study, communal prayer and festivals (Yom Kippur, Pesach) may be considered more important expressions of Jewish identity, involving the whole community and addressing the most fundamental aspects of the covenant. Many deeply committed Jews (including Reform and Liberal) do not observe kashrut strictly yet maintain a rich Jewish identity through prayer, community and ethical action. Non-religious view: A humanist might argue that cultural identity is expressed through community, shared memory and ethical values rather than dietary rules. Justified conclusion required. Mastering: Balanced, developed; sources on both sides; non-religious view; conclusion. Secure: Both sides, source, conclusion. Developing: One side. Emerging: Listing, no conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Naomi is preparing her home for Pesach. Give one thing she needs to do before the festival begins.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for one correct preparation. Acceptable answers: remove all chametz (leavened bread and products) from the home; buy matzah for the festival; prepare the Seder plate with its symbolic foods; arrange the family Seder meal and the reading of the Haggadah.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation?
A) The bread and wine are symbols of Jesus's body and blood
B) Jesus is spiritually but not physically present in the Eucharist
C) The substance of the bread and wine truly becomes the body and blood of Christ at the consecration
D) The Eucharist is a re-enactment of the Last Supper but nothing actually changes
practice_questions.marks: C) The substance of the bread and wine truly becomes the body and blood of Christ at the consecration [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the Catholic sacrament described as 'the source and summit of Christian life'.
practice_questions.marks: The Eucharist (also accept 'the Mass') [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Give two contrasting Christian beliefs about what happens after death.
For each belief, give a brief development.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per belief (1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point).
Acceptable points include:
- Catholic teaching includes belief in purgatory — a process of purification for those who die in God's grace but are not yet ready for heaven; Catholics therefore pray for the souls of the dead, particularly on All Souls' Day.
- Most Protestant Christians reject purgatory, arguing that Christ's atoning death is fully sufficient — at death, those who have faith enter immediately into the presence of God (2 Corinthians 5:8); praying for the dead is therefore not a Protestant practice.
- Orthodox Christianity teaches ongoing development toward God after death (theosis) but uses different terminology from purgatory.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the seven sacraments are important for Catholic Christians.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two fully developed reasons; at least one named source (e.g. Matthew 26:26-28 for the Eucharist, John 6:51, the Nicene Creed); both reasons clearly connected to significance for Catholic life.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two reasons present, accurate; source cited but not fully developed.
Developing (2 marks): One reason developed or two briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1 mark): Basic relevant point; no source.

Acceptable points include:
- The sacraments are the primary means through which God communicates grace to believers — without the sacraments, Catholics believe they would be cut off from the divine life; baptism removes original sin and initiates believers into the Church, making all subsequent sacramental life possible.
- The Eucharist, described as 'the source and summit of Christian life', makes the sacrifice of Christ present at every Mass (Matthew 26:26-28: 'This is my body... this is my blood'); this means Catholics can participate directly in Christ's redemptive act week by week.
- Reconciliation (confession) restores the relationship with God broken by serious sin — it reflects Jesus's words to the disciples: 'If you forgive anyone's sins, their sins are forgiven' (John 20:23).

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in purgatory is the most important Catholic teaching about life after death.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Catholic teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Balanced evaluation; accurate Catholic teaching on resurrection, judgement, heaven, hell and purgatory; Protestant rejection of purgatory cited and developed; named sources (1 Corinthians 15:3-4, the Nicene Creed, Catechism teaching); justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present; source included; conclusion reached but weighing of arguments incomplete.
Developing (4-6 marks): One-sided or both sides briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points, no sources, no conclusion.

Arguments in support:
- Purgatory is distinctively Catholic — it shapes a range of practices (prayer for the dead, indulgences, masses for the souls of the deceased) that are absent from Protestant Christianity; it could be argued that this makes it uniquely defining for Catholic identity.
- Purgatory expresses the Catholic belief in God's mercy toward those who have tried to live well but are imperfect — it offers hope for the majority of believers who are not fully ready for heaven at death.
- The doctrine shapes how Catholics grieve: the practice of praying for the dead (especially on All Souls' Day) gives a practical dimension to belief that is absent if purgatory is rejected.

Arguments against:
- The resurrection is arguably more foundational — the Nicene Creed, which Catholics recite at every Mass, includes 'I look forward to the resurrection of the dead' but does not mention purgatory; resurrection is thus doctrinally more central.
- Most Protestant Christians reject purgatory entirely, regarding it as lacking biblical support; this means it is a divisive rather than a unifying belief and might not be 'most important' if measured by breadth of Christian agreement.
- For many Catholics, the belief in heaven — eternal communion with God — is more important because it is the ultimate destination and the source of Christian hope.

Conclusion: Candidates may reasonably argue either side. A strong conclusion acknowledges that purgatory is distinctive to Catholicism but that the resurrection and heaven are more central to the Catholic creed as recited at Mass.

practice_questions.text:
Patrick is preparing to receive the sacrament of Confirmation at his Catholic parish in Manchester. Give two effects that Confirmation is believed to have, according to Catholic teaching.
For each effect, give a brief development.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per effect (1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point).
Acceptable points include:
- Confirmation strengthens the faith received at baptism.
- It is believed to confer the gifts of the Holy Spirit on the recipient.
- It completes the initiation into the Church begun at baptism.
- It equips the confirmed Catholic to be a witness to their faith in the world.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes Pikuach Nefesh?
A) A Jewish dietary law forbidding pork
B) The principle that saving a human life overrides almost all of the mitzvot
C) A festival celebrating the Exodus from Egypt
D) A form of daily prayer recited three times a day
practice_questions.marks: B) The principle that saving a human life overrides almost all of the mitzvot [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the Hebrew term for the Jewish concept of 'healing the world'.
practice_questions.marks: Tikkun olam [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give one way in which the principle of Pikuach Nefesh affects Jewish life in practice.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for one correct example. Examples: a Jewish doctor or nurse may work on Shabbat to save a life; non-kosher food may be eaten if it is the only available way to survive; an ambulance driver who is Jewish will drive on Shabbat to reach an emergency. The rule applies across Orthodox, Reform and Liberal communities.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the concept of tzedakah is important in Jewish life.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed reasons, each with clear explanation and a named source. Strong sources: Deuteronomy 16:20 ('Justice, justice shall you pursue'); Talmud Sanhedrin 37a; the teaching that tzedakah is rooted in tzedek (justice) not generosity. Sub-tradition application adds depth: e.g. how Reform synagogues organise food banks as a community mitzvah. Secure: Two reasons present, source cited but not fully developed. Developing: One reason developed, source named but not linked. Emerging: Basic points, no source.

practice_questions.text:
'Pikuach Nefesh is the most important moral principle in Judaism.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Jewish teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
